title: the jewel and the guru's son
hookLine: a mother sits down and refuses to eat until she sees the jewel from her sons' killer's head
carry: kshama: Draupadi takes the jewel, not his life

cards: Morning. Dhrishtadyumna's charioteer, one of the few who got away, brings the news to Yudhishthira, and the king falls to the ground. Then Draupadi comes.
Her brother is dead. Her five sons are dead. She sits down in front of her husbands and says she'll take no food until Ashvatthama pays for this.
And she names what she wants. Ashvatthama was born with a jewel on his head. She wants to see it brought back, and worn by Yudhishthira.

teach.h: THE WEAPON IN A BLADE OF GRASS
teach.b: Bhima rides out at once. Krishna warns that Drona once taught his son a terrible weapon, the Brahmashira, and Ashvatthama is reckless enough to use it. So Krishna, Arjuna and Yudhishthira follow.
They find Ashvatthama on the bank of the Ganga, among sages, with Vyasa. He charges a blade of grass with that weapon and lets it go. Arjuna answers with the same.
Two fires rise, and the sages Narada and Vyasa step between them to save the world. Arjuna, who has kept his vows, calls his weapon back. Ashvatthama can't.
He turns it toward the unborn heirs of the Pandavas, and Krishna answers that Uttara's child will live, because Krishna will revive him.
Then Krishna curses Ashvatthama to wander the earth alone for a very long time, and Ashvatthama gives up the jewel he was born with. Now watch Draupadi. Her brother and her sons are dead.
In Ganguli's telling she says, in effect, that she only wanted the wrong answered, and that a teacher's son deserves the reverence due the teacher.

She takes the jewel, not his life, and gives it to Yudhishthira to wear. The Bhagavata Purana tells it more tenderly still: there Draupadi asks that he be spared, so his mother won't weep as she is weeping.
Hindus call this kshama, forgiveness, and count it among the great virtues. It doesn't pretend the wrong didn't happen. It asks what needs to be answered, and lets the rest go.

how: Ashvatthama's wandering under Krishna's curse is told in retellings of the epic, and some Hindus tell stories of him still wandering the earth.

o: the sage who sits with Ashvatthama by the Ganga
the night book, which ends with a jewel carried to Draupadi
the weapon Drona taught his son, charged in a blade of grass

games.q: by the Ganga — tap the pairs.

s: Ashvatthama called his weapon back when the sages stood between
he couldn't, and turned it toward the wombs of the Pandava women.
the jewel from Ashvatthama's head went to Yudhishthira
Draupadi gave it to Yudhishthira, and he wore it.
in the end, Draupadi asked that Ashvatthama be killed
when the jewel came, she said a teacher's son deserves reverence, and gave it to Yudhishthira.

games.q: you're Draupadi. the jewel from Ashvatthama's head is in your hands, and your sons are gone. what do you do?
o: honor him as your teacher's son and give the jewel to the king.
throw the jewel into the Ganga.
games.why: she gives the jewel to Yudhishthira and honors Drona's son: the wrong answered, the life spared. Hindus call that kshama.

practice: At the end of a puja, many Hindus say a short prayer asking forgiveness for anything done wrong in it. Bring your palms together. Bring to mind someone who owes you something, or someone you owe.
Breathing in, name what needs to be made right. Breathing out, name what you could let go. If you pray, you can leave the rest in God's hands.

wordCard.voice: Sauptika. The night book ends by the Ganga: two weapons, two sages, a curse, and a jewel taken instead of a life.

orig.note: jewel: the gem on Ashvatthama's head that Draupadi asks for.
